records.description: Orbital electron capture consumes a bound electron in a specified nuclear transition and emits an electron neutrino; in the selected 140Pr to 140Ce channel it converts a proton to a neutron, preserves mass number A=140 and lowers nuclear charge Z from 59 to 58. Initial bare 140Pr59+, hydrogenlike 140Pr58+ and heliumlike 140Pr57+ carry zero, one and two bound electrons respectively. EC removes one bound electron while lowering Z by one, so the daughter ionic charge remains the same. Changing the initial ionization state does not change which parent isotope is prepared; the subsequent nuclear decay does change the element.

records.description: In the leading coherent ultrarelativistic vacuum model with hbar=c=1, hold U, L and E fixed. Replacing every m_i^2 by m_i^2+kappa multiplies A_alpha-to-beta by exp[-i kappa L/(2E)], leaving P=|A|^2 unchanged. This holds for shifts preserving m_i^2+kappa>=0 and (m_i^2+kappa)/E^2<<1. For three nonnegative squared masses, Delta21=m_2^2-m_1^2 and Delta31=m_3^2-m_1^2 both nonzero and unequal imply three pairwise distinct values; at most one can be zero, so at least two masses are nonzero.
records.name: Oscillation mass identifiability
openObligations: This is a conditional algebraic consequence of the declared leading vacuum phase, not a new measurement, global fit or independent replication of mass splittings. Fixed preparation, energy and detector response are assumed; endpoint kinematics, time of flight, coherence conditions and higher-order dispersion are not covered by this invariance.

An admissible common shift changes the absolute mass scale without changing these probabilities. No unique absolute masses, measured upper bound, mass ordering, Dirac versus Majorana character or mass-generation mechanism follows from this statement. Keeping the ultrarelativistic approximation valid is not an experimentally inferred upper bound.

Two nonzero differences alone are insufficient: (m_1^2,m_2^2,m_3^2)=(q,0,0), q>0, gives Delta21=Delta31=-q and only one nonzero mass. The unequal-differences condition excludes this degeneracy. Conversely (0,a,b), with a,b>0 and a!=b, meets the condition while one mass is zero; all three need not be nonzero.

The three-state and nonnegative-mass assumptions are explicit. Separate historical effective two-flavor fits are not automatically a joint closed three-state likelihood; their best-fit numbers are not identified here with exact three-state splittings or pooled into new constraints.

openObligations: BRDF has units sr^-1, while R=pi*f_r is a dimensionless directional reflectance factor relative to an ideal unit-reflecting Lambertian diffuser. Neither is an integrated reflected-energy fraction; a factor above one is not by itself an energy-conservation violation.

Use the actual finite-spot, finite-aperture, spatial-uniformity and polarization conditions. The effective projected solid angle includes cos(theta_r) and finite-size/collection-efficiency corrections; a raw detector-voltage ratio is not a calibrated BRDF.

Absolute ratio measurement means normalization to measured incident flux rather than a reference sample. It still requires monitor, relative-gain, angle, aperture, collection and sample-uniformity calibration; it is not calibration-free.

Nominal directional-hemispherical reflectance, bidirectional reflectance factor and a whole angular distribution are different. One integral or one direction does not determine the other or uniquely identify microscopic roughness, composition, shape or a scene.

A rough or porous target can have subsurface contributions. These data do not uniquely separate surface from volume scattering, reconstruct a complete electromagnetic boundary solution or measure crystallinity as a necessary cause.

The preceding remote-sensing example mentions viewing near40 degrees; the actual reported Figure11 measurement uses45 degrees. Nominal99/10 percent directional-hemispherical labels are not independent measured Lambertian directional values.

The source uses linearly polarized illumination and supplies a separate s/p averaging rule. Most systematic components are highly correlated between polarizations; unpolarized uncertainty is not automatically reduced by treating s and p as independent replicates.

The out-of-plane uncertainty estimates are rough, target- and geometry-specific, and larger angle/solid-angle contributions are expected than for the tabulated in-plane calibration examples. No full covariance or universal precision is newly reconstructed.

Reference-mirror/PTFE spectral scans and ROSI-STARR comparisons in this publication reuse the same named standards and calibration chain. They are not independent new studies for every wavelength, sample or instrument; the earlier STARR publication was not newly read.

The exact microscopic reason for the Figure11 deviations is not resolved by the source. No raw signal/angle recalibration, curve digitization, fitted surface model, sensor-image experiment or scene-reconstruction accuracy is supplied.

The Figure11 caption and selected Section6.B account do not state whether its curves use s polarization, p polarization or an unpolarized average. The general linear-source/averaging method does not fix that missing preparation detail, and no particular Figure11 polarization state is inferred.
